key: Thus saith the LORD: Cursed is the man that trusteth in man, And maketh flesh his arm, And whose heart departeth from the LORD.
s: Setting a desert shrub against a watered tree, the chapter pronounces a curse; Radak, on 17:5, reads the curse as resting on the heart that turns away, for relying on a man is no evil if one holds he helps only by God’s aid.

evidence.gloss: [On ‘and whose heart departeth from the LORD’:] for if his heart does not turn from the LORD, it is no evil if he trusts in a man to help him, provided his intention is that a man can help only with God’s help and not otherwise.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Jeremiah 17:5, at [416,5]). Plain sense faithful: 17:6 likens the one cursed to a tamarisk in the desert and 17:8 the one blessed to a tree planted by the waters, framing the curse of 17:5; no four-word repeat of the key. Radak’s comment on the lemma ‘and whose heart departeth from the LORD’ makes the turning of the heart the ground of the curse and says trusting a man for help is no evil when one holds that a man helps only by God’s aid; the reading says that and no more. Rashi (sabbatical-year trust) and Metzudat David differ in emphasis but do not contradict. Entry passes entry-check.
